q-149679.name: Question 1
q-149679.problem:
The closed, positively oriented curve $C$ is defined as $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as

$$
n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.
$$

Find the function $a(t).$
q-149679.worked_solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

q-126922.problem: The closed curve $C$ is defined as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=5.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
q-126922.worked_solution:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{5},
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].

q-149681.problem:
The closed, positively oriented curve $C$ is defined as $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as

$$
n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.
$$

Find the function $b(t).$
q-149681.worked_solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=\frac{7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $b(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$

The closed curve C is defined as r(t)=5sin⁡ti+11cos⁡tj for t∈[0,2π). The outward-pointing unit normal vector for C can be expressed as

n=a(t)i+b(t)j||r′(t)||. Find the function a(t).

Hint: Observe that C is traversed clockwise.

a
5sin⁡t
b
11cos⁡t
c
−5cos⁡t

e

EXPLANATION

For convenience, we express r(t) in column vector notation:

r(t)=[x(t)y(t)]=[5sin⁡t11cos⁡t]

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, negatively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

Step 1: We compute the tangent vector r′(t).

Differentiating the expression for r(t), we get

r′(t)=[x′(t)y′(t)]=[5cos⁡t−11sin⁡t].

Step 2: Since C is oriented clockwise, we rotate r′(t) by 90∘ counterclockwise to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a 90∘ counterclockwise rotation is

R=[0−110].

Rotating the vector r′(t) by 90∘ counterclockwise, we get

[0−110][5cos⁡t−11sin⁡t]=[11sin⁡t5cos⁡t].

Step 3: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of r′(t) (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

n=1||r′(t)||[11sin⁡t5cos⁡t]=11sin⁡ti+5cos⁡tj||r′(t)||.

Finally, we conclude that a(t)=11sin⁡t.

q-149684.name: Question 8
q-149684.problem:
The closed curve $C$ is defined as $r(t)=7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector for $C$ can be expressed as

$$
n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.
$$

Find the function $a(t).$

*Hint: Observe that $C$ is traversed clockwise.*
q-149684.worked_solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

To calculate the outward normal vector of a closed, *negatively* oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented clockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *counterclockwise* to obtain an outward normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=\frac{9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=9\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]

$$

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise rotation is

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

The closed curve $C$ is defined as $r(t)=9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector for $C$ can be expressed as

For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, *negatively* oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented clockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *counterclockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise rotation is

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}10\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}10\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=\frac{10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=10\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
